notes: Costs appeal on reasonableness of instructing London libel specialists after mistaken paedophile photograph publication; Eady J dismissed on review.

enrichment.short_title: Gazley v Wade: costs appeal on instructing London libel specialists
key_facts: The Sun published Mr Gazley's photograph beside captions wrongly identifying him as a paedophile; liability was admitted and damages were settled after Carter-Ruck replaced local solicitors Belmores.
Costs Judge Simons held it was not reasonable to instruct specialist London firm Carter-Ruck because only damages and apology remained outstanding.
The appeal was heard by Eady J with assessors on review principles under CPR 52.11 and Wraith v Sheffield Forgemasters.
The claim settled via offer of amends and Part 36 for £50,000 after Carter-Ruck's involvement.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal with assessors from a detailed assessment decision on the reasonableness of instructing specialist London solicitors.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the costs judge's conclusion that instructing Carter-Ruck was unreasonable on these unusual facts was not wrong.
enrichment.ratio: On a costs appeal by way of review the court asks whether the costs judge was wrong, not whether it would have decided differently; reasonableness of instructing specialist solicitors is judged at the time of the decision and on the particular facts, applying Wraith criteria without laying down general libel guidelines.
legal_issues: Whether a costs judge erred in holding instruction of London libel specialists unreasonable
Application of Wraith criteria and CPR 52.11 review standard
Whether new evidence on Belmores' advice should be admitted on appeal
Whether the case was wrongly categorised as a Norfolk rather than national libel matter
linked_authorities: Wraith v Sheffield Forgemasters Limited [1998] 1 WLR 132
Solutia UK Limited v Griffiths [2001] EWCA Civ 736
Musa King v Telegraph Group Limited [2004] EWCA Civ 613

notes: POCA cash detention extension timing and directory notice rules; Divisional Court allowed Chief Constable's appeal.

enrichment.short_title: Merseyside Police v Reynolds: POCA cash detention period calculation

statutes_considered.title: Magistrates' Courts (Detention and Forfeiture of Cash) Rules 2002

key_facts: Merseyside Police seized about £14,980 and forged US dollars from Mr Reynolds under section 294 POCA 2002.
Justices extended detention for 90 days from 11 February 2004 but refused a further extension on 11 May because they held the earlier order expired at 10:00 am and Form A notice was defective.
The Chief Constable appealed by case stated on when the 90-day period ended and whether Rule 5's seven-day notice requirement was mandatory.
The Divisional Court held the detention order expired at midnight on 11 May and Rule 5(3) was directory.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Divisional Court appeal by case stated from Liverpool Justices refusing continued cash detention.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; justices had jurisdiction, the February order expired at midnight on 11 May, and the matter was remitted to a different bench.
enrichment.ratio: When calculating a fixed period from an order date the start day is excluded so a 90-day detention from 11 February expired at midnight on 11 May; procedural notice requirements in Rule 5 are directory and non-compliance does not destroy jurisdiction where the respondent attended without prejudice.
legal_issues: Whether a timed detention order expires at the same clock time or at midnight on the final day
Whether failure to give seven days' notice under Rule 5 irretrievably flaws the application
Application of Marren v Dawson Bentley and Dodds v Walker to POCA detention periods
linked_authorities: Marren v Dawson Bentley & Co Ltd [1961] 2 QB 135
Dodds v Walker [1981] 1 WLR 1027
R (Halford) v Colchester Magistrates' Court (25 October 2000)

notes: Leading tax appeal on sections 555-556 ICTA entertainers regime and extraterritorial collection against foreign payers.

enrichment.short_title: Agassi v HMRC: sports endorsement tax and territoriality principle
key_facts: Andre Agassi, a non-UK resident tennis player, received endorsement payments from Nike and Head through his US company Agassi Enterprises for UK tournament activities.
HMRC assessed him under section 556 attributing payments to the sportsman despite payment to his company.
Agassi argued section 555(2) collection duties did not apply to payers with no UK tax presence, so section 556(2) was disapplied by section 556(5).
The Court of Appeal allowed the appeal, reversing Lightman J.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal from High Court upholding Special Commissioners on UK taxation of foreign sports endorsement income.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; Agassi was not to be treated as recipient of Nike and Head payments to Enterprises.
enrichment.ratio: The territoriality principle in Clark v Oceanic Contractors applies to section 555(2) collection obligations on foreign payers without UK presence; unenforceable extraterritorial duties should not be implied, and section 556(5) excludes attribution where no section 555(2) obligation arises.
legal_issues: Whether section 555(2) applies to foreign companies with no UK tax presence
Interaction of sections 555, 556 and 556(5) in the entertainers and sportsmen code
Whether Schedule 11's purpose required disapplication of the territoriality principle
Whether section 555(2) applies to all section 18 payments in a consolidating statute
linked_authorities: Clark v Oceanic Contractors Inc [1983] 2 AC 130
Agassi v HM Inspector of Taxes [2004] EWHC 1022 (Ch)
Ramsay v IRC [1982] AC 557

notes: NUJ judicial review on Schedule A1 para 35 blocking recognition where rival union had voluntary agreement.

enrichment.short_title: NUJ v CAC: voluntary recognition agreement blocking statutory claim

statutes_considered.title: Trade Union and Labour Relations (Consolidation) Act 1992

key_facts: The NUJ sought statutory recognition for MGN Sports Division journalists with majority support after MGN planned seven-day Racing Post publication.
MGN secretly signed a voluntary recognition agreement with the rival BAJ, which had at most one member in the unit.
The CAC ruled the NUJ application inadmissible under paragraph 35 because a collective agreement was already in force with BAJ.
The NUJ challenged the decision as incompatible with Article 11 ECHR and argued 'in force' required implementation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court judicial review of CAC decision refusing admissibility of statutory trade union recognition application.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; paragraph 35 was correctly construed, the BAJ agreement was in force, and Article 11 imposed no duty to recognise the majority union.
enrichment.ratio: Paragraph 35 excludes CAC jurisdiction where a collective agreement recognising another independent union is already in force; recognition is a bilateral employer-union act not requiring workforce consent, and Article 11 does not require employers to recognise a particular union where another is voluntarily recognised.
legal_issues: Meaning of 'already in force' in Schedule A1 paragraph 35
Whether 'on behalf of' workers requires union representativeness
Article 11 ECHR compatibility of the exclusionary rule
Construction of collective agreement under section 178
linked_authorities: Wilson and National Union of Journalists v UK [2002] IRLR 568
R (Kwik-Fit (GB) Ltd) v Central Arbitration Committee [2002] EWCA Civ 512
Attorney General's Reference No 4 of 2002 [2004] UKHL 43

notes: GMC Health Committee appeal on alcohol dependence diagnosis and medical assessor role; Silber J dismissed.

enrichment.short_title: Boodoo v GMC: alcohol conditions and F10.2 diagnosis fairness

statutes_considered.title: General Medical Council Health Committee (Procedure) Rules Order of Council 1987

key_facts: Dr Boodoo appealed conditions imposed by the GMC Health Committee for 24 months restricting his practice due to alcohol misuse.
Psychiatrists had classified harmful use (ICD F10.1) but the committee found alcohol dependence syndrome (F10.2) without prior notice.
The doctor had repeatedly breached undertakings to abstain and showed liver damage with heavy drinking before the hearing.
He challenged fairness of the F10.2 label and alleged medical assessors exceeded their advisory role.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal under section 40 Medical Act 1983 from GMC Health Committee fitness-to-practise conditions.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed with £5,000 costs; the committee's findings were supported by uncontradicted expert evidence.
enrichment.ratio: Where three psychiatrists' uncontradicted evidence established strong desire to drink, difficulty controlling intake and persistent harmful use, the committee could properly impose alcohol limitation conditions even if the F10.2 label was not expressly raised; medical assessors may advise on medical significance under Schedule 2 paragraph 5 without supplying new factual evidence.
legal_issues: Whether finding ICD F10.2 without express notice breached natural justice
Scope of medical assessors' duty under Schedule 2 paragraph 5
Whether alcohol consumption limitation conditions were supported by evidence
Standard of review of GMC Health Committee decisions
linked_authorities: Nwabueze v General Medical Council [2000] 1 WLR 1760
Ghosh v General Medical Council [2001] 1 WLR 1915
R (M) v Criminal Injuries Compensation Panel [2001] EWHC Admin 720

notes: Will validity appeal on testamentary capacity and knowledge and approval; Court of Appeal upheld 1994 will.

enrichment.short_title: Hoff v Atherton: testamentary capacity and knowledge of will changes
key_facts: Mrs Krol, an elderly widow with about £1 million assets and mild dementia, made a 1994 will leaving residue to neighbour Mrs Atherton instead of godson Francis Hoff and others under her 1987 will.
A deputy judge upheld the 1994 will finding testamentary capacity and knowledge and approval despite signs of cognitive decline.
Independent solicitor Mr Hatt read the will aloud at execution; Mrs Atherton had helped obtain planning permission but undue influence was not pleaded.
The claimants appealed arguing actual understanding and knowledge of the change from the prior will were required.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal from probate judgment pronouncing for validity of 1994 will and against 1987 will with codicils.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; Mrs Krol had testamentary capacity and knew and approved the 1994 will's contents.
enrichment.ratio: Testamentary capacity requires ability to understand the nature of the act, the extent of property and claims on bounty, not proof of actual understanding in every case; knowledge and approval is distinct and where a beneficiary assisted preparation suspicion is dispelled if the testator understood the straightforward dispositions, without always requiring explicit comparison with a prior will.
legal_issues: Whether doubtful capacity requires proof of actual understanding under Banks v Goodfellow
Whether knowledge and approval requires the testator to be told of significant changes from an earlier will
Inference of capacity from execution circumstances and witness evidence
Effect of beneficiary involvement in will preparation under Fuller v Strum
linked_authorities: Banks v Goodfellow (1870) LR 5 QB 549
Fuller v Strum [2002] 1 WLR 1087
Masterman-Lister v Brutton & Co [2003] 1 WLR 1511

notes: Permission to appeal refused on GP's disclosure of medical records to MDU solicitor for assault proceedings.

enrichment.short_title: Mensah v Jones: medical records disclosure to defence solicitor
key_facts: Dr Jones removed Mr Mensah from his patient list after a surgery incident and retained computer records while paper records went to a new practice.
In separate assault proceedings Dr Jones printed medical records and sent them to his MDU solicitor for disclosure advice.
Mr Mensah sued in a second action claiming breach of confidentiality and data protection law.
Deputy Master Lloyd granted summary judgment for Dr Jones and permission to appeal was refused.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for permission to appeal from summary judgment and refusal of permission on paper.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal refused; disclosure to the doctor's solicitor for legal proceedings was necessary and lawful.
enrichment.ratio: Section 35(2) Data Protection Act 1998 exempts disclosure necessary for legal proceedings; a doctor may send confidential records to his solicitor to obtain advice on disclosure obligations in related litigation, and section 13 damages for distress require damage or special purposes processing.
legal_issues: Whether section 35(2) exempts disclosure of medical records to a doctor's own solicitor
Applicability of section 7 subject access rights without written request
Whether common law confidentiality precludes litigation-related disclosure to legal advisers
Availability of damages under section 13 for distress alone

notes: Habitats Regulations licence appeal on whether species preservation is overriding public interest under reg 44(2)(e).

enrichment.short_title: Newsum v Welsh Assembly: great crested newt relocation licence
key_facts: Duke of Westminster trustees sought a regulation 44 licence to translocate great crested newts from Pen-yr-Henblas quarry before possible reopening under existing planning permission.
The Welsh Assembly refused, finding no current overriding public interest in quarrying and that species preservation alone was not an imperative reason under regulation 44(2)(e).
Pitchford J quashed the refusal; the Assembly appealed.
The quarry had permission but no immediate reopening plan and CCW might have been the appropriate authority under regulation 44(2)(c).
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal from judicial review quashing refusal of habitats regulations derogation licence.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; preservation of the species itself is not an imperative reason of overriding public interest under regulation 44(2)(e).
enrichment.ratio: Regulation 44(2)(e) covers projects with overriding public interest that incidentally harm protected species, not conservation of the species itself, which falls under regulation 44(2)(c); the existence of planning permission does not itself establish imperative overriding public interest for an (e) licence.
legal_issues: Whether species preservation can be an imperative reason of overriding public interest under regulation 44(2)(e)
Overlap between regulation 44(2)(c) and (e) licensing purposes
Relevance of extant planning permission and regulation 40(3)(c) lawful operation defence
Whether the Assembly could ignore arguable non-criminal quarrying under regulation 40

notes: Landmark Mareva/freezing order case holding banks owe claimants a duty of care once served with notice.

enrichment.short_title: Customs v Barclays: bank duty of care on freezing orders
key_facts: HM Customs obtained freezing orders against Brightstar and Doveblue for unpaid VAT, identifying Barclays accounts holding substantial credit balances.
After faxed notice of the orders Barclays permitted large Faxpay transfers out due to operator error and system bypass before acknowledgment letters were received.
Customs obtained judgments and garnishee orders but recovered far less than the debts because accounts had been depleted.
Colman J held at preliminary issue that Barclays owed no duty of care; the Court of Appeal reversed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal on preliminary issue whether a bank served with a freezing injunction owes the claimant a duty of care.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; declaration that Barclays owed Customs a duty of care when the payments were made in breach of the orders.
enrichment.ratio: Once a bank is served with notice of a freezing order the relationship with the claimant is sufficiently proximate and it is fair, just and reasonable to impose a duty to take reasonable care to prevent dissipation of frozen funds; contempt remedies are inadequate and banks are expected under Z Ltd v A-Z to preserve assets, with assumption of responsibility not always required.
legal_issues: Whether proximity arises without express assumption of responsibility when a freezing order is served
Whether contempt jurisdiction displaces tortious duty on third-party banks
Application of Caparo threefold test to economic loss claims
Timing of duty: service of order versus acknowledgment letter
linked_authorities: Z Ltd v A-Z and AA-LL [1982] QB 558
Caparo Industries plc v Dickman [1990] 2 AC 605
Henderson v Merrett Syndicates Ltd [1995] 2 AC 145
